opus-5.5.text:
I think that explanation is a big part of it, and it's the one Hans Moravec himself offered. The things we find effortless, like picking up a cup, walking across a cluttered room, or folding a towel, are things our ancestors were refining for hundreds of millions of years, long before anything like abstract reasoning showed up. Chess and calculus are very recent additions, so they feel hard to us, and it turns out they're comparatively easy for computers. The sensorimotor stuff is so deeply optimized in us that it's invisible. We don't notice how hard it is.

But I don't think evolution is the whole story. Part of it is also about the physics of the problem. When you're manipulating objects in the real world, you have uncertainty everywhere: in sensing, in control, and in the physical properties of the objects themselves. Friction, mass distribution, how a deformable object like a cable or a piece of cloth will behave. Tiny errors at the fingertip get amplified. You can't perfectly model those contact interactions, even in principle, because they depend on microscopic surface details you can't observe. So it's not just that we had a head start. The domain itself is fundamentally noisy and chaotic in a way that board games and text are not.

The other piece, which matters a lot right now, is data. Large language models had the entire internet to learn from, essentially trillions of tokens. For robots, there's no equivalent. We don't have an internet-scale corpus of robot actions with the forces and contacts recorded. Some people estimate the gap at something like 100,000 years' worth of data. Evolution gave humans that data implicitly, through countless generations of trial and error. Robots have to acquire it somehow, whether through simulation, teleoperation, or video, and each of those has real limitations.

So I'd say the evolutionary explanation is correct, but it's best understood as pointing at two deeper facts: physical interaction is intrinsically hard because of uncertainty, and humans got an enormous amount of embodied training that we're only beginning to approximate. That's why I tend to urge some caution when people predict that general-purpose humanoid robots are just around the corner. Progress is real and exciting, but Moravec's paradox is still very much with us.

r001.rationale: It describes the task-difficulty disparity and separately labels evolution, physical uncertainty, and data as explanations for it.

r002.rationale: It contrasts chess and calculus as comparatively easy for computers with everyday sensorimotor tasks that are easy for humans but difficult for robots.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's basically right, and it's the explanation Moravec himself gave. The idea is that the things that feel effortless to us — picking up a cup, walking across a cluttered room, folding a shirt — feel effortless precisely because evolution has been optimizing them for hundreds of millions of years. We don't have conscious access to how hard they are. Whereas the things we think of as hard, like chess or calculus or symbolic reasoning, are very recent. They're maybe a few thousand years old in our evolutionary history, so we experience them as effortful, and it turns out they're actually the easier ones to formalize and hand to a machine.

So I find the evolutionary story compelling as far as it goes. But I'd add a couple of things to it. One is that it's not just that we've had a long time to evolve these skills — it's that the physical world is genuinely, intrinsically hard in ways that abstract domains aren't. In chess, the state is fully observable, the rules are known, and nothing is uncertain. In the physical world, you've got friction, you've got deformable objects, you've got sensor noise, you've got occlusion — you reach into a bin and you literally can't see what's behind the thing in front. And the physics of contact is still something we can't model very precisely. So part of why manipulation is hard for robots is not only that we're competing against a highly evolved opponent; it's that the problem itself is full of uncertainty and we don't have clean models of it.

The second thing I'd say is that the evolutionary explanation is a little bit too comforting, in a sense, because it can suggest that if we just had enough time or enough data, we'd close the gap. And I'm skeptical of that framing. Evolution had a very particular kind of training signal — survival over a huge number of embodied agents interacting continuously with the real world. We don't have that for robots. We can't collect physical interaction data at anything remotely like internet scale, the way we did for language. That's really the crux of why language models leapt ahead and robots didn't. The text was already there; the robot experience isn't.

So, to sum up: I think the evolutionary explanation is a real and important part of the story, but I'd pair it with the point that the physical world is just hard — hard in a way that doesn't go away even if you understand where our own skills came from.

r002.rationale: It contrasts effortless human physical skills such as walking and grasping with formal tasks such as chess and calculus, explaining that physical skills are hard for robots while abstract tasks are easier to formalize for machines.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a plausible explanation, though I’m not sure it’s the whole story. Perception and physical coordination have a very long evolutionary history, and much of what makes them work is invisible to us. You pick up a cup without consciously thinking about where to place your fingers, how much force to apply, or how to adjust if it starts slipping. When we try to get a robot to do it, all those hidden difficulties become apparent.

But I’d be cautious about treating evolution as a complete explanation. Saying that we’ve had millions of years to develop those abilities gives us an intuition for why they’re sophisticated; it doesn’t necessarily tell us which parts are hard to reproduce, or how to reproduce them. That’s what we have to discover by building systems and seeing where they fail.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a plausible explanation. Moravec’s paradox is that things we think of as intellectually difficult, like playing chess, turned out to be relatively easy for computers, whereas things that a child can do, like picking up an unfamiliar object, are still very difficult for robots.

And the evolutionary argument is that perception and movement have been under development for hundreds of millions of years. We’re not consciously aware of most of the computation involved. We just reach out and pick up a cup. But that apparent simplicity hides an enormous amount of sophistication.

I’d be cautious about treating that as a complete explanation, though. It gives us an intuition for why these skills might be difficult to reproduce; it doesn’t tell us exactly what’s missing or how to build it. For robotics, that’s the interesting question: how do we turn that observation into systems that can reliably deal with the physical world?

r001.rationale: It describes the paradox as a pattern in task difficulty, then separately presents evolution as a proposed explanation and notes it may be incomplete.

r002.rationale: It contrasts chess, described as intellectually difficult for people but relatively easy for computers, with picking up an unfamiliar object, easy for a child but difficult for robots.
